chapters.title: Chapter 15 · A Golden Picnic
chapters.artPrompt: four girls with baskets picnicking on a flat mossy stone in a maple wood of gold and scarlet leaves, a hilltop view of bright sea beyond fields, crisp golden October light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: October came in gold, and the maple woods by the shore road turned into treasure. The Story Club declared a holiday picnic, and four girls set out one Saturday with baskets: Anne, Diana, Ruby Gillis, and Jane Andrews. Davy begged to come along, and was consoled with the last of the cookies. The morning was so bright that even the frogs looked pleased.
Four friends and two baskets in the golden maple woods.

They ate lunch on a flat mossy stone, with sandwiches and cookies and story talk. Ruby told the newest news twice, for practice. Jane described her future house, which would have every modern improvement. Diana said exactly what Anne was thinking. Anne talked of books and Redmond and all the years ahead. For once, nobody quarreled, not even over the last cookie — Davy was not there.
Talk together: If your friends planned a golden-day picnic, what would go in the baskets — and who would tell the stories?

After lunch they climbed the hill through the maples, where every leaf was a small sun. From the top they could see the sea, a thin bright line beyond the fields. A hawk circled once over the hilltop and sailed away to sea. The wind smelled of apples and falling leaves. Nobody said much for a while, because some afternoons are too good for talking, and this was one of them.

They came home at sunset, when the lanes were bars of gold, with their arms full of scarlet and amber leaves. Marilla said the house smelled of October for a week, and swept leaves out of every corner. Even Mrs. Lynde approved of the leaves, which was rare praise. Anne pressed the handsomest leaf in her dictionary, where she kept treasures. Years afterward, finding it there, she smiled. That day, she said, had been made of the very stuff happy memories are woven from.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 · Goodbye, Ruby
chapters.artPrompt: a young woman with red braids sitting beside a pale girl lying among white pillows by a curtained bed, a small vase of autumn flowers on the table, soft late afternoon light through white curtains, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One soft autumn day, word came that Ruby Gillis was ill, and it was the kind of illness that does not go away. She had been the prettiest girl in school, fond of red ribbons and admirers. Now the doctor shook his head. Anne went at once, carrying flowers, and found Ruby lying very small and white among the pillows.
Anne sits by Ruby's white-curtained bed in the late afternoon light.

Ruby talked first of old times — picnics, beaux, and school jokes. Anne talked of old school days until Ruby smiled at the ceiling. Then Ruby's voice shook a little. She was frightened, she owned, of what was coming. 'Don't go yet,' she begged, so Anne stayed until the lamp burned low. Anne held her hand the whole time, and by and by Ruby's fear grew quiet, like wind settling at evening.
Talk together: Ruby was afraid, and being with her friend made her less afraid. What can we give someone who is frightened — besides advice?

When Anne went home, the stars were out over Green Gables, and she sat a long time by her window. Somewhere an owl called, very softly. She thought of Ruby's laughing eyes, and of how quickly even long summers end. Ruby Gillis died before the week was out, quietly, in her sleep. Avonlea could not believe it. The prettiest girl in the village had gone, and the world seemed a plainer place.

Marilla found her crying quietly and did not scold. 'You loved her, and you'll miss her,' said Marilla. 'That is what loving people costs.' Diana came over that evening, and the two friends sat close together without needing many words. Anne dried her eyes and made herself a quiet promise: to live with twice as much care, for those who could not stay to see the summers come. It was a promise she never quite forgot.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 · Echo Lodge Afterward
chapters.artPrompt: a small white-haired lady in a soft apron comforting a tearful little maid in a starched apron among shining pans in a cozy lodge kitchen, roses visible through the open door, warm hearth light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Echo Lodge was lonely no longer. Miss Lavender had come home with her tall husband, and the old garden had never heard so much laughter. The gate stood open half the day for callers, and there were callers every day. Stephen Irving wrote at his desk among the roses, and Miss Lavender sang over her baking like a girl of seventeen.
The kitchen at Echo Lodge, bright with baking, books, and laughter.

But one small person at the lodge was not laughing. Charlotta the Fourth, the little maid, had served Miss Lavender faithfully for years. She had secretly feared the wedding would send her away. Her real name was Leonora, but nobody at the lodge ever used it. She went about so long-faced that even the cat noticed. At last Miss Lavender caught her wiping her eyes with her apron among the pans.
New word: faithfully — doing a thing steadily and loyally, day after day. Talk together: how do you show someone their work matters to you?

'Charlotta,' said Miss Lavender, sitting down beside her among the pans, 'did you think I would send my Charlotta away?' And she laughed her old laughing laugh, and kissed the little maid on both cheeks. 'This lodge needs you more than ever. Who else knows exactly how I like everything in this house?' Charlotta the Fourth beamed through her tears, and from that day she bustled prouder than any maid in Avonlea.

Paul came over the fields nearly every day now, between his grandmother's house and the lodge, and called both places home. In the evenings he read his compositions aloud to his father and Miss Lavender and Charlotta the Fourth, who cried at the sad parts. He was careful to praise every story equally, which was wise of him. And in the garden at dusk, Miss Lavender still liked to talk to the echo. But now, whichever way she called, somebody always answered back.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 · The Walks with Gilbert
chapters.artPrompt: a tall boy and a girl with red braids walking and talking along a country lane past ripe orchards and red maples, their shadows long on the dusty road, low golden evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Gilbert Blythe walked part of the way home with Anne on still autumn evenings, and those walks had become the best part of her week. The air smelled of ripe apples, and the maples burned red along the fences. Their shadows walked beside them, very long in the low light. They argued about books, about words, about everything under the sun. Gilbert was going to Redmond College too, and they studied the same lessons, which gave their arguments sharp edges.
Two friends and one long dusk on the road past Mr. Harrison's fields.

Once upon a time, a boy had called Anne 'carrots' and pulled her hair. She had smashed her slate over his head, and the quarrel lasted years. Now it seemed so far away that it was mostly a family joke. Diana said they could argue the paint off a fence, which was true. 'We were very silly,' Anne admitted one evening. 'We were,' said Gilbert cheerfully, 'and then we grew up, which is the whole point of school.'
Talk together: Anne and Gilbert were rivals for years before they were friends. Can a rival teach you anything a friend cannot?

He teased her about her daydreams, then listened to every one of them seriously. He lent her his best books and never asked for them back on time. When she doubted whether she was clever enough for college, he laughed at the very idea, so warmly that she could not go on doubting. A friend like that, Anne thought, was better than a dozen admirers.

They parted at the Green Gables gate each evening, he down the road, she up the lane, always with one more thing to say. Anne wrote in her diary that Gilbert Blythe was no longer her rival. He was her friend — and friendship, she suspected, was the rarer treasure of the two. Then she underlined it twice, in red ink, because some things deserve red ink.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 · The Last Day of School
chapters.artPrompt: a young woman with red braids looking back from a green lane at a small white schoolhouse with a bell tower, a chalked farewell on the step, flowers heaped at the door, bright June morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: At last a bright June morning came when the school term ended, and Anne's days as Avonlea's teacher were done. It felt strange and sweet at once. The pupils came carrying armfuls of flowers, until her desk was a small garden. Even Anthony Pye brought a fistful of daisies and looked fiercely embarrassed about it.
The last assembly, with the teacher's desk hidden under flowers.

There were songs, and a great deal of sniffing in corners. Paul Irving read a farewell composition that set everybody off again, especially Anne. The trustees shook her hand and said the school had never done better. Diana came to watch from the back bench, remembering old days. Then the little ones crowded round her, and she shook every small hand in the room.
Talk together: Anne taught every grade in one small school, from first letters to long essays. What would be the best part of a job like that — and the hardest?

When the children had gone, she rang the bell once more, just to hear it. Then she locked the schoolhouse door and gave the key to the trustees. She walked down the lane without looking back — for about twenty steps. Then she had to look. Somebody had chalked a wobbly GOODBYE on the step. The white schoolhouse stood in the June light, its little tower clear against the sky, and every window flashed as if it winked.

She had gone into that school a frightened girl of sixteen, pretending to be dignified. She came out of it knowing how to keep order, how to say sorry, and how forty faces could become forty friends. She had turned over her own new leaf, more than once. It had been hard, funny, tiring work, and she would not have missed a day of it. Whatever Redmond might bring, she would carry her teaching years with her like a smooth grey pebble in her pocket, cool and lasting.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 · The Road to Redmond
chapters.artPrompt: a girl with red braids beside a packed trunk at the gate of a green-gabled farmhouse, an older woman in grey and a stout older woman waving from the door, a boy with a fishing rod watching from a fence, clear September morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The trunk stood packed in Anne's room, and Green Gables was in a gentle uproar. Mrs. Rachel Lynde and Marilla between them could run Green Gables better than ever, they declared. There were last instructions about the hens, and last warnings about Davy. Davy announced that he meant to cry all week, and then went off fishing instead, twice in one morning. Dora cried a little and then bravely rearranged the pantry, which was her way of being upset.
Anne's trunk by the Green Gables door on a September morning.

The night before she left, Gilbert came to the gate, and they walked down the lane in the low gold light. They knew every root and bend of that lane, and slowed down on purpose. Redmond College lay ahead of them both, with years of work and new faces beyond it. 'The old rivalry is dead,' said Anne. 'Long live the friendship,' said Gilbert. They shook hands across the gate like two small nations signing a treaty.
Talk together: Anne is leaving home for school, with her family waiting at Green Gables. What would you pack in one trunk to take a little bit of home along?

In the morning Marilla stood very straight at the gate. She did not cry until the last moment — and then cried anyway. Anne hugged her hard, and Marilla said something about her collar being crumpled, which meant much more. Mrs. Lynde pressed a parcel of doughnuts into Anne's hands for the journey. Dora had slipped a folded note of good wishes into the trunk, spelled perfectly.

And so Anne Shirley rode away toward Redmond and whatever came next. Behind her lay the fields she knew by heart, the white schoolhouse, and all her seasons of pupils and paint pots, twins and pine trees. Growing up, she had discovered, was not the end of the adventure at all. It was only more road, with the morning sun on it, and a friend going the same way.
